Home accessibility or multigenerational renovation tax credit: the CAD 20,000 and CAD 50,000 limits, the end of the medical double claim, and where each renovation dollar should go

A renovation that adds a ramp, a walk-in shower or a secondary suite for a parent can fall under three federal credits: the home accessibility tax credit, the refundable multigenerational home renovation tax credit and the medical expense tax credit. Each expense can count only once, and from 2026 that includes the medical and accessibility pair. This guide sets out the limits and who qualifies, then finds the split of a renovation’s costs that returns the most, with charts for refundability, the 2025 and 2026 rules, and CRA’s claim statistics.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 27 October 2026 · 9 min read
Sources reviewed 27 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

For 2026, with $60,000 of work, the best split the calculator finds is to put $45,000 into the multigenerational home renovation tax credit (MHRTC), $15,000 into the home accessibility tax credit (HATC) and $0 into the medical expense tax credit (METC). At the 14% rate that returns $8,400.00: $6,300.00 refundable and $2,100.00 of non-refundable credits. From 2026 an expense claimed as a medical expense is no longer a home accessibility expense, so each dollar goes to one credit only. Putting everything into the MHRTC gives $7,000.00; keeping the accessibility features out of it gives $8,400.00. Under 2025 rules the same work would return $9,526.50. Provincial credits, a spouse’s or relative’s separate claims and the eligibility tests themselves are not modelled; CRA decides the claims.

The central idea

The home accessibility tax credit (HATC, line 31285) returns the lowest federal rate on up to CAD 20,000 a year of renovation costs for a person aged 65 or more or eligible for the disability tax credit; it is non-refundable. The multigenerational home renovation tax credit (MHRTC, line 45355) returns the same rate on up to CAD 50,000 for building a self-contained secondary unit so that such a person can live with an adult relative; it is refundable, claimed in the year the work is finished, and available once in that person’s lifetime. An expense in the MHRTC claim cannot also be claimed for the HATC or medical expense credit, and from 2026 an expense claimed as a medical expense no longer counts for the HATC either. The rate is 14.5% for 2025 and 14% for 2026, so the maximums are CAD 2,900 and 7,250 for 2025 and CAD 2,800 and 7,000 for 2026. In the default 2026 example, keeping CAD 15,000 of accessibility features out of a CAD 45,000 secondary-unit claim returns CAD 8,400 instead of CAD 7,000.

01

Three credits, one renovation

When a family adapts a home for an older parent or an adult with a disability, the bills often cover two kinds of work: building a self-contained space and making it safe to use. Federal tax law has a credit for each, and a third, the medical expense tax credit, covers some of the same items. The credits pay the same rate but have different limits, different refund rules and, since 2026, stricter rules against counting one expense twice. Which credit each dollar is claimed under can change the result by more than a thousand dollars.

The calculator takes a renovation’s cost in three parts: the secondary unit itself, the accessibility and safety features, and the part of those features that is also a medical expense. It finds the split that returns the most, and compares it with two simple approaches: putting everything into the multigenerational credit, or keeping the accessibility features out of it.

02

What each credit covers

Home accessibility tax credit (HATC)Multigenerational home renovation tax credit (MHRTC)
Line31285, non-refundable45355 with Schedule 12, refundable
For whomA qualifying individual: 65 or older at the end of the year, or eligible for the disability tax credit at any time in the yearA qualifying individual: 65 or older at the end of the year, or 18 to 64 and eligible for the disability tax credit
What workEnduring renovations that let that person get into, move around or function in the home, or that reduce the risk of harm thereA renovation that creates a secondary unit, with its own entrance, kitchen, bathroom and sleeping area, so that person can live with a qualifying relation (an adult parent, grandparent, child, grandchild, sibling, aunt, uncle, niece or nephew)
LimitCAD 20,000 of expenses a year per qualifying individual, and per dwelling if several live thereCAD 50,000 of expenses per qualifying renovation; one renovation per qualifying individual for life
When claimedIn the year the expenses are paid or incurredIn the year the renovation is completed, including costs from earlier years
RateThe lowest federal rate: 15% to 2024, 14.5% for 2025, 14% for 2026

Both exclude routine repairs and maintenance, household appliances, home-entertainment electronics, housekeeping and gardening services, financing costs and work by a relative who is not registered for GST/HST. The HATC also excludes items that can be used independently of the renovation and work done mainly to raise the home’s value. Sources: CRA line 31285, CRA MHRTC eligibility, MHRTC expenses and the Income Tax Act, section 118.041 and section 122.92.

03

Counting an expense once: what changed for 2026

CRA’s line 31285 page, written for 2025 returns, says an expense that qualifies as both a medical expense and a home accessibility expense can be claimed as both. A walk-in bathtub for someone with a severe mobility impairment can therefore count twice for 2025. CRA’s Budget 2025 page describes the change: for 2026 and later years, an expense claimed under the medical expense tax credit is excluded from the HATC. The consolidated Act now carries it as paragraph (k) of the definition of qualifying expenditure in section 118.041, added by S.C. 2026, c. 3, s. 42.

The MHRTC was always exclusive. CRA’s how-to-claim page says expenses included in an MHRTC claim cannot be claimed for the medical expense credit or the HATC. So from 2026 each renovation dollar can go to one of three places, and the choice turns on the limits, the medical expense threshold, and whether the claimant owes enough tax to use a non-refundable credit.

04

How the calculator splits the costs

All three credits pay the same rate, so a dollar is worth the same in any of them as long as it fits under a limit and can be used. The differences come from four places:

  • The MHRTC limit. Above CAD 50,000 of claimed costs, an extra dollar in the MHRTC returns nothing. Accessibility features that push a secondary unit over that limit are better claimed under the HATC.
  • The HATC limit. Only CAD 20,000 a year counts. Features above that are better in the MHRTC if it has room.
  • The medical expense threshold. The medical credit applies only to expenses above the lesser of 3% of net income and CAD 2,834 for 2025 or CAD 2,890 for 2026. A medical item claimed there loses the threshold amount unless other medical expenses have already used it; the same item under the HATC does not.
  • Refundability. The HATC and medical credits can only reduce tax to zero. The MHRTC is paid even when no tax is owed.

The calculator tries every CAD 500 step of the accessibility costs moved into the MHRTC, together with the exact limit and endpoint values, and for 2026 the points at which medical items should move between the medical credit and the HATC. It reports the split with the largest total.

In the first case the unit alone uses CAD 45,000 of the MHRTC’s CAD 50,000, so CAD 10,000 of the features would earn nothing there; under the HATC all CAD 15,000 counts. The fourth case under 2025 rules would return CAD 4,306.50, because the CAD 10,000 of medical items could count for both credits. In the last case, the best split moves CAD 30,000 of non-medical features into the MHRTC to fill it and leaves the rest for the HATC, so every dollar is credited at 14%. 06

Timing: calendar years and the completion year

The HATC limit is per calendar year, but the MHRTC is claimed once, in the year the renovation is completed, at that year’s rate. Two consequences follow.

  • A renovation that spans December and January can use two years of HATC limits for features paid in each year, up to CAD 40,000 in total, while the secondary unit’s costs from both years go into one MHRTC claim.
  • A renovation started in 2025 and finished in 2026 is an MHRTC claim on the 2026 return, at 14%. CRA’s own example is a renovation begun in April 2025 and completed in July 2026, claimed for 2026.

CRA treats the renovation period as starting with the first qualifying expense (for example, a building permit) and ending when the work is completed, for example on passing final inspection. The qualifying individual and the relative must ordinarily live in the home within 12 months after that.

07

How many people claim the home accessibility credit

CRA’s final statistics show 37,410 returns claiming home accessibility expenses for the 2023 tax year, for CAD 229.3 million in total, about CAD 6,129 per return. The peak in the series available here was 2022, with 47,130 claims, the first year the limit doubled to CAD 20,000. Averages of CAD 4,000 to 6,000 suggest most claims are for modest work rather than full renovations. CRA counts returns, not households, so a couple who split one renovation appear twice. The same 2023 table has the first year of the MHRTC: 6,040 returns claimed CAD 22.0 million of the refundable credit, about CAD 3,648 each. At that year’s 15% rate, that is the credit on about CAD 24,300 of renovation costs per return, roughly half of the CAD 50,000 limit.

08

Before you claim

  1. Check who qualifies first. The HATC needs a person aged 65 or more or eligible for the disability tax credit; for someone under 65, a DTC approval (Form T2201) must be in place. The MHRTC needs a new, self-contained unit that meets local by-laws.
  2. Keep invoices that separate the work. CRA asks for the contractor’s name, business address and GST/HST number, a description of the work and goods, the dates and proof of payment. Separate lines for the ramp, bathroom and unit make it possible to allocate them.
  3. Decide which return carries which credit. The HATC can be claimed by the qualifying individual or by an eligible family member; the MHRTC by any eligible individual who incurred costs, up to CAD 50,000 together. A relative who owes more tax may get full use of the non-refundable HATC.
  4. Watch the year. For 2026 a medical expense item cannot be claimed under the HATC as well; plan which one it goes to.
  5. Look for provincial credits. Some provinces have their own home accessibility or renovation credits; they are separate from the federal ones covered here.

09

What the calculator leaves out

  • Eligibility. It assumes every condition is met, including the relationship, ownership, occupancy within 12 months and, for the MHRTC, that no earlier claim exists for the same person.
  • Several claimants. It models one claimant. Splitting the HATC or MHRTC among family members, and the medical credit for a dependant, can change the result.
  • The exact tax. The tax owed is entered by you. The calculator does not compute federal tax, provincial tax or other credits.
  • Which items are medical expenses. Renovation costs count as medical expenses only in specific cases, such as for a person with a severe and prolonged mobility impairment; the calculator takes the amount you enter.
  • Grants. Government grants do not reduce the HATC, but other reimbursements reduce both credits, and for the MHRTC CRA says any assistance or rebate reduces the expenses.
  • Years. Only 2025 and 2026 rules are included.
